actors.name: DPRK-linked coordinated ATM cash-out networks
actors.description: North Korean state-directed operations that compromise a bank's payment switch or card processing environment, force fraudulent authorisation responses, and then simultaneously withdraw cash from ATMs across many countries using pre-positioned mule networks. It is the purest hybrid in this database: the intrusion is remote and the extraction is entirely physical, requiring hundreds of people standing at machines in coordinated time windows. US CISA and Treasury have issued repeated advisories.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The scenario that most clearly defeats a siloed security model. Detection depends on correlating switch anomalies with ATM withdrawal patterns in near real time, which requires the fraud, cyber and ATM operations functions to share telemetry. Losses are realised in minutes across dozens of jurisdictions and are effectively unrecoverable.
ttps: Intrusion into payment switch and card processing infrastructure
Malicious applications forcing fraudulent authorisation responses on behalf of the issuer
Pre-positioning of mule networks in many countries with cloned cards
Simultaneous timed withdrawals across jurisdictions, usually on weekends or holidays
Rapid consolidation and laundering of proceeds through crypto and cash couriers
Targeting of institutions in jurisdictions with weaker switch segmentation

existence.basis: CISA, FBI and Treasury advisories; multiple confirmed incidents.

attribution.basis: Formally attributed to DPRK by US and allied governments.

financial_targeting.basis: Banks and their ATM estates are the sole target.

state_tasking.basis: Government attribution to DPRK revenue generation programmes.

notable_incidents.summary: A single incident saw simultaneous cash withdrawals from ATMs in more than 20 countries; another involved withdrawals across 30 countries.

watch_indicators: Switch or HSM configuration changes outside change windows
Authorisation responses inconsistent with core banking balances
Withdrawal clusters on a small set of BINs across many countries
Elevated activity on a public holiday or weekend

sources.title: CISA Alert: FASTCash 2.0 / North Korea's BeagleBoyz Robbing Banks

actors.name: POS terminal swap and merchant-side tampering cluster
actors.description: Crews that substitute a merchant's payment terminal with a tampered unit, or open and modify a terminal in situ, to harvest card data at the point of acceptance. Access is obtained either by posing as maintenance engineers or by recruiting merchant staff. It is quieter and higher yield than ATM skimming because compromise can persist for months without any customer-visible symptom.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Directly attacks the acquirer's estate and the merchant relationship, and it is frequently discovered only through common-point-of-purchase analysis rather than physical inspection. Acquirers carry the reconciliation, remediation and merchant remediation cost, and the insider dimension means terminal logistics and engineer identity verification are the real controls.
ttps: Impersonation of terminal maintenance engineers to gain physical access
Substitution of a genuine terminal with a pre-modified unit
In-situ opening and implanting of a data-capture module
Recruitment or bribery of merchant staff to permit or ignore access
Interception of terminals in the distribution and repair supply chain
Periodic revisits to harvest stored data

existence.basis: Long-running acquirer and law enforcement casework internationally.

attribution.basis: Perpetrators are diverse and rarely form persistent groups.

financial_targeting.basis: Payment acceptance infrastructure is the sole target.

watch_indicators: Terminal serial numbers not matching deployment records
Unscheduled engineer visits reported by merchants
Common-point-of-purchase concentration at a single merchant
Tamper-evident seal discrepancies at routine servicing

sources.title: EAST: Data relay attacks drive up European terminal related fraud incidents

actors.name: Coerced-withdrawal and ATM duress cluster
actors.description: Offenders who abduct or restrain a victim and drive them between ATMs, forcing withdrawals up to daily limits, sometimes across a rollover at midnight to double the take. Known as express kidnapping in Latin America, it also appears in European night-time economy areas as a short-duration variant following a street robbery.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The clearest case where transaction monitoring can detect an in-progress violent crime rather than just a loss. Repeated maximum withdrawals across multiple machines in a short window, especially spanning midnight, is a recognisable and actionable signature. Some institutions have implemented duress-aware limits and referral rules on this basis.
ttps: Abduction or restraint following a street robbery or ride-hail interaction
Sequential withdrawals across several ATMs to defeat single-machine limits
Deliberate continuation across the midnight limit rollover
Coercion of card and PIN disclosure through threat or violence
Use of the victim's own vehicle for movement between machines

existence.basis: Well-documented across Latin America, Africa and parts of Europe.

financial_targeting.basis: The ATM network is the extraction mechanism.

watch_indicators: Sequential maximum withdrawals at multiple ATMs within a short period
Withdrawals spanning the midnight limit reset
Withdrawal geography inconsistent with the customer's normal pattern
Failed PIN attempts immediately preceding successful maximum withdrawals

sources.title: EAST European Payment Terminal Crime Report

actors.name: Targeted violence against financial sector executives and staff
actors.description: A convergent pattern rather than a single actor: organised crime coercing compliance and investigations staff, ideologically motivated attacks on named executives, grievance-driven lone actors, and kidnapping of banking personnel for ransom in high-kidnap jurisdictions. The common feature is that the individual, not the institution, is the attack surface, and that home addresses and family details are the targeting data.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Executive and staff protection has moved from a niche concern to a core financial-sector security discipline, driven by three developments: cheap brokered violence in the Nordics and Australia, doxxing and open-source targeting, and the willingness of networks like the Mocro Maffia to attack officers of the justice system. Data protection of staff personal information is now a physical security control, not just a privacy one.
ttps: Open-source and breach-derived collection of home addresses, vehicles and routines
Surveillance of residences and predictable movements
Commissioned assault, arson or shooting via intermediaries
Kidnapping for ransom of executives and their families in high-risk jurisdictions
Threats and harassment against compliance, collections and foreclosure staff
Coercion to obtain access, information or favourable decisions

existence.basis: Multiple documented cases across the jurisdictions listed.

attribution.basis: Perpetrators range from state-linked to organised crime to lone actors; brokered violence deliberately obscures the commissioner.

financial_targeting.basis: Financial sector individuals are one of several professional target groups, alongside lawyers, journalists and officials.

notable_incidents.summary: Killing of lawyer Derk Wiersum demonstrated Dutch organised crime's willingness to attack officers of the justice system, a precedent directly relevant to financial crime investigators.

watch_indicators: Staff personal data appearing in breach dumps or on hostile forums
Employee reports of surveillance, unexpected deliveries or approaches
Escalating grievance correspondence naming individual staff
Institution named in an active hostile campaign

sources.title: Murder of Derk Wiersum
The Com: Theft, Extortion, and Violence are a Rising Threat to Youth Online (IC3 PSA)

actors.name: Data centre and technology supply-chain physical intrusion cluster
actors.description: Physical approaches to the compute and network estate underpinning financial services: intrusion into colocation facilities, tailgating on contractor credentials, theft of drives and equipment, and interference with power and cooling. State-linked pre-positioning against operational technology has been documented, but the higher-frequency reality is theft and contractor-mediated unauthorised access.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The physical layer of a bank's technology estate is largely operated by third parties with their own vetting standards, and access is mediated by contractor identity processes rather than the bank's. This is a genuine control gap: institutions audit their cloud providers' certifications but rarely test who can physically stand next to their racks.
ttps: Tailgating and use of contractor credentials to enter colocation halls
Theft of drives, network equipment and decommissioned hardware
Interference with power, cooling and fire suppression systems
Interception or substitution of equipment in the logistics chain
Reconnaissance of facility layout, plant and access control

existence.basis: Documented intrusion and theft incidents; state pre-positioning documented in critical infrastructure OT more broadly.

attribution.basis: Most incidents are unattributed; conflation of criminal theft with state pre-positioning is a known analytical error.

financial_targeting.basis: Facilities are shared; finance-specific targeting is generally inferred rather than demonstrated.

watch_indicators: Access log anomalies at colocation facilities hosting the institution's estate
Contractor credential sharing or unescorted access findings in audits
Equipment discrepancies at decommissioning or asset reconciliation
Drone activity or reconnaissance reported at the facility

sources.title: Admitting the Elephantine Void Between Kinetic and Cyber Threats
UK and allies uncover Russian military unit carrying out cyber attacks and digital sabotage

actors.name: Cash courier and bulk value movement cluster
actors.description: The physical movement of cash, gold and bearer value across borders by human couriers, vehicle concealment and air cargo, underpinning almost every laundering typology in this database. It is the point at which criminal proceeds are most physically vulnerable, which is also why couriers are themselves robbed, and why courier robbery is a recurring feature of organised crime violence.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The bridge between the physical crime economy and the banking system. Institutions encounter it as structured deposits after a courier run, as MSB counterparties with volumes inconsistent with their corridor, and as customers whose businesses exist to justify cash. FinCEN has specifically warned about cartel repatriation of bulk cash through armoured car and air transport services.
ttps: Human couriers carrying cash and gold on commercial flights and land crossings
Vehicle concealment and use of legitimate freight for bulk movement
Exploitation of armoured car and air cargo services for repatriation
Structuring of subsequent deposits across many branches and institutions
Hawala and informal value transfer settlement to avoid movement entirely
Recruitment of insiders at ports, airports and cargo handlers

existence.basis: FinCEN advisories, customs seizure data, prosecutions worldwide.

attribution.basis: Couriers are interchangeable and rarely connect to identifiable principals.

financial_targeting.basis: Banking and MSB rails are the destination for the value moved.

notable_incidents.summary: FinCEN alert on cross-border bulk cash smuggling from the United States into Mexico, noting cartel use of armoured car services and air transport.

watch_indicators: Structured deposits following known courier corridor timing
MSB corridors with volumes far exceeding the size of the diaspora served
Customs seizure notifications naming a customer or counterparty
Cash-intensive customers whose declared trade cannot generate the volume

sources.title: FinCEN Warns US Financial Institutions of Bulk Cash Smuggling Risks from Mexico-Based Cartels
Money laundering crime in Australia - AFP

actors.name: Branch siege, hostage and grievance-driven attack cluster
actors.description: Incidents in which an individual, usually acting alone and often a customer rather than a professional criminal, takes over a bank branch. Motivations range from robbery to grievance over frozen deposits or foreclosure. Lebanon's 2022 wave of depositors storming branches to withdraw their own frozen savings, some of them publicly celebrated, is the clearest modern illustration that this category is driven by systemic conditions as much as by individual pathology.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The scenario branch staff are most likely to actually face, and the one where security posture interacts most directly with reputational risk, because the assailant may be a sympathetic figure. Response planning has to account for the possibility that public opinion sides with the person holding the branch, which changes both the police response and the aftermath.
ttps: Lone actor entering with a weapon or claimed device during opening hours
Detention of staff and customers to compel a withdrawal or extract publicity
Grievance framing communicated to media during the incident
Escalation triggered by delay or perceived deception in negotiation
Imitation clustering following a publicised incident

existence.basis: Recurring documented incidents across many jurisdictions.

attribution.basis: Predominantly lone actors with no organisational affiliation.

financial_targeting.basis: Bank branches are the deliberate location.

notable_incidents.summary: Repeated incidents in which depositors, some armed, seized branches to force withdrawal of their own frozen savings amid the banking crisis; several attracted public sympathy rather than condemnation.

watch_indicators: Escalating grievance correspondence or branch confrontations by a named customer
Systemic events affecting deposit access or foreclosure volumes
Publicised incident at a peer institution creating imitation risk

sources.title: Bank Robbery News - FBI

actors.name: Private security and cash-logistics industry infiltration cluster
actors.description: Deliberate placement or recruitment of personnel inside guarding companies, cash-in-transit operators and ATM service providers. Because these firms compete on price, vetting quality is uneven and turnover is high, and they hold precisely the schedule, route and value information that makes a high-value physical attack feasible. Almost every large CIT and cash centre loss in this database has an insider component.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Financial institutions outsource the function but retain the loss. The practical implication is that vetting standards, access segregation and information compartmentation at the contractor are a bank control problem, and contractually specifying them is more effective than any physical hardening the bank can buy.
ttps: Placement of associates into guarding and CIT roles through legitimate recruitment
Recruitment of existing staff through debt, community ties or coercion
Extraction of route timings, load values, alarm states and key control procedures
Facilitation of access during an attack, including disabling of controls
Exploitation of high turnover and subcontracting chains to defeat vetting

existence.basis: Recurring feature of major CIT and cash centre prosecutions internationally.

attribution.basis: Insiders identified case by case; recruiting networks often not.

financial_targeting.basis: Recruitment targets roles with access to cash, keys and schedules.

watch_indicators: Contractor staff churn without corresponding vetting evidence
Access to schedules or CCTV beyond role requirements
Unexplained affluence or debt resolution among cash-access staff
Subcontracting chains that obscure who actually holds the keys

sources.title: Highway Bandits, An Ever Increasing Trend In European Armed Robbery

actors.name: Shareholder meeting and corporate event disruption cluster
actors.description: Coordinated disruption of annual general meetings, investor days and sponsored events by climate, human rights and anti-war campaigners, using proxy attendance, blockades of venue access, and disruption from the floor. Distinct from branch actions because participants often have a legal right to be present, which constrains the response options available to the institution.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: A predictable, date-bound physical security requirement with an unusual constraint: many disruptors are legitimate shareholders. It creates governance-visible reputational risk, and venue and executive movement security around these dates is a recurring cost. Because the dates are published, this is the most plannable item in the whole database.
ttps: Acquisition of shares to obtain legitimate AGM attendance rights
Coordinated interventions from the floor and banner deployment
Blockade of venue entrances and lock-on devices
Targeting of sponsored events, conferences and art or sport sponsorships
Pre-briefed media coverage timed to the event

existence.basis: Extensively documented at major financial institutions' AGMs.

attribution.basis: Actions are publicly claimed by named campaigns.

financial_targeting.basis: Financial institutions' governance events are the deliberate target.

watch_indicators: Campaign announcements referencing the AGM date
Unusual small share purchases before the record date
Actions at peer institutions' AGMs in the same season

sources.title: Barclays banks superglued shut in nationwide action against climate criminals

actors.name: Synthetic-media-enabled physical intrusion and courier fraud cluster
actors.description: Use of cloned voices and synthetic video to obtain physical outcomes: authorising a courier collection, instructing a facilities team to admit a contractor, approving an out-of-band cash release, or persuading a customer to hand over value at the door. The important shift is that synthetic media is increasingly used to move a physical process rather than to complete a purely digital transaction.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: It undermines voice and video as verification for exactly the processes that were deliberately moved off digital channels for safety, including out-of-band callbacks for high-value payments and physical access authorisation. Institutions that responded to payment fraud by adding a human voice check have, in some cases, added an attack surface rather than removed one.
ttps: Voice cloning of executives to authorise urgent payments or access
Synthetic video in conference calls to legitimise instructions
Impersonation of bank staff to direct customers to hand over cards or cash
Manufactured urgency to defeat callback and cooling-off controls
Combination with courier collection to complete extraction physically

existence.basis: Multiple confirmed corporate incidents and law enforcement warnings.

attribution.basis: Perpetrators are usually offshore and unidentified.

financial_targeting.basis: Payment authorisation and bank identity are the targets.

watch_indicators: Out-of-band authorisation requests originating from an unfamiliar number
Urgent instructions that discourage independent verification
Facilities or courier access authorised verbally without written confirmation
Customers reporting convincing calls from apparent bank staff

sources.title: Six jailed for more than 25 years after GBP 1 million courier fraud

actors.name: Crypto kiosk physical attack and tampering cluster
actors.description: Physical attacks on cryptocurrency kiosks, including removal of the whole unit, forced opening of the cash box, and tampering to capture user credentials or redirect deposits. Kiosks are attractive because they hold cash but are typically deployed in low-guardianship retail with far less protective engineering than bank ATMs.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Relevant to institutions that bank kiosk operators, and as a leading indicator for the security standards regulators will eventually impose. It is also a useful contrast case: the kiosk sector shows what an ATM estate looks like without the accumulated physical security standards the banking industry developed over decades.
ttps: Removal of the whole kiosk from unsecured retail locations
Forced opening of the cash acceptor and note store
Tampering to capture wallet addresses or redirect deposits
Targeting of sites with no attendant presence outside trading hours

existence.basis: Reported incidents and operator advisories; less systematically tracked than bank ATM crime.

financial_targeting.basis: Kiosks hold cash and crypto value; the sector is adjacent to rather than part of regulated banking.

watch_indicators: Kiosk operator customers reporting repeated unit losses
Insurance claims concentrated on a single operator's estate
Deployment into sites with no anchoring or attendant presence

sources.title: Crypto kiosk fraud topped $389M in 2025

actors.name: Disaster, unrest and outage exploitation cluster
actors.description: Exploitation of civil unrest, natural disaster or extended power and telecoms outage to attack branches and ATMs while police and alarm response are saturated or unavailable. It is opportunistic rather than organised, but the losses are concentrated: a single unrest event can destroy dozens of machines and multiple branches in a night.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The scenario in which every response-dependent control fails simultaneously. Alarm monitoring, guard response and police attendance all assume ordinary conditions. Planning for it means accepting that during the event nothing can be protected, and concentrating on cash withdrawal from the estate beforehand and rapid restoration afterwards.
ttps: Attack on branches and ATMs during unrest when response is saturated
Exploitation of extended power or telecoms outage disabling alarms
Forced entry through fire-damaged or already-breached premises
Secondary looting of adjacent commercial premises

existence.basis: Repeatedly documented during major unrest events internationally.

financial_targeting.basis: Branches and ATMs are attacked as available high-value targets, not selected in advance.

watch_indicators: Civil unrest forecasts and protest scheduling in branch catchments
Extended grid or telecoms outage affecting alarm reporting
Attacks on adjacent commercial premises as an escalation signal

sources.title: EAST European Payment Terminal Crime Report

actors.name: Accelerationist infrastructure-attack networks
actors.description: Transnational neo-Nazi accelerationist networks that promote attacks on electricity infrastructure as a deliberate strategy to precipitate societal collapse. The Terrorgram Collective functioned as a publishing and radicalisation layer rather than an operational cell structure, distributing target guidance and celebrating attacks. Its two US-based leaders were arrested in September 2024, and Atomwaffen Division founder Brandon Russell was convicted in February 2025 and sentenced in August 2025 to 20 years for conspiring to destroy electrical facilities serving Baltimore. More than a dozen separate federal prosecutions involve alleged core members or individuals inspired toward infrastructure attacks.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Relevant in two ways, and it is worth being precise about which. Directly, the ideology is antisemitic and explicitly anti-financial, so banks appear in propaganda target lists alongside synagogues, power stations and data centres, and staff who are publicly identifiable are within the threat model. Indirectly and more probably, the strategy of attacking electricity infrastructure to induce cascading failure puts the institution's continuity planning, not its guard force, in the line of fire. Attack planning is amateur but intent is explicit and published, which makes it unusually legible for a threat of this severity.
ttps: Online publication of target guidance, substation lists and attack methodology
Planned rifle attacks on transformers at multiple substations serving a single metro area
Explosive and incendiary device plots against energy facilities
Attempted use of drones carrying explosive payloads against substations
Radicalisation and tasking of isolated individuals with no organisational contact
Celebration of unattributed attacks to encourage imitation

existence.basis: Multiple US federal convictions and indictments; UK and other proscription action against related entities.

attribution.basis: Named defendants convicted; the Collective's leadership publicly identified and charged.

financial_targeting.basis: Financial institutions appear in propaganda but no executed attack in this dataset targeted one; the realistic exposure is grid dependency.

notable_incidents.summary: FBI arrested Dallas Humber and Matthew Allison, the two US-based leaders of the Terrorgram Collective, on charges including conspiracy, soliciting hate crimes and distributing bomb-making instructions.
Atomwaffen Division founder Brandon Russell convicted of conspiring to destroy Baltimore-area power stations; sentenced in August 2025 to 20 years.
Skyler Philippi pleaded guilty to attempting to use a weapon of mass destruction and to destroy an energy facility, having planned a drone-borne explosive attack on substations.

watch_indicators: Institution or named staff appearing in accelerationist propaganda or target lists
Substation attack plots reported in the utility service area
Federal charging announcements indicating an active regional cell
Drone sightings over energy infrastructure serving the institution

actors.name: State-sponsored OT pre-positioning in critical infrastructure
actors.description: PRC state-sponsored intrusion into the IT environments of communications, energy, transportation and water utilities, with US authoring agencies assessing with high confidence that the objective is pre-positioning for lateral movement into operational technology in order to disrupt functions during a future crisis. Tracked as Volt Typhoon by CISA and as VOLTZITE by Dragos, among numerous vendor names. It belongs in a physical threat database because the intended effect is physical: the loss of power, water or communications, not the theft of data.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: This is the case the Elephantine Void argument is really about. What is established is presence in utility IT networks and an assessed intent to reach OT. What is not established is any executed disruption, and conflating the two overstates the position. For a bank the practical exposure is identical to the grid attack cluster and should be planned for the same way, as dependency on utilities that may fail without warning and without a weather explanation. The distinctive addition is that a state-timed outage would be simultaneous across regions, which defeats mutual-aid and failover assumptions built around localised events.
ttps: Living-off-the-land techniques using built-in tools to avoid detection
Compromise of small office and edge network devices as operational relays
Long-dwell persistence in utility IT networks without data exfiltration
Reconnaissance of OT asset inventories, network diagrams and control systems
Credential harvesting from domain controllers for durable access
Targeting of communications and energy providers serving strategically significant regions

existence.basis: Joint CISA/NSA/FBI advisory AA24-038A and independent vendor tracking by Dragos and others.

attribution.basis: Formally attributed to PRC state sponsorship by US and allied agencies.

financial_targeting.basis: Finance is not among the sectors named as compromised; exposure is entirely via dependency on affected utilities.

state_tasking.basis: Government attribution states PRC sponsorship and assesses pre-positioning intent with high confidence.

notable_incidents.summary: CISA, NSA, FBI and partners issued AA24-038A documenting compromise of communications, energy, transportation and water sector IT environments across the continental US, its territories and Guam, assessing pre-positioning for OT disruption.

watch_indicators: Advisories naming utilities or telecoms serving the institution's sites
Simultaneous unexplained outages across geographically separate regions
Utility disclosure of intrusion affecting operational technology
Edge device compromise notifications from network providers

actors.name: Hardware and firmware supply-chain tampering cluster
actors.description: Physical modification of hardware or firmware somewhere between manufacture and deployment: implanted devices added to servers, network gear, ATMs, HSMs and payment terminals; firmware flashed during manufacture, repair or shipping interdiction; or rogue devices attached to a network by someone who walked in. This is the category where public claims and public evidence diverge most sharply. The 2018 Bloomberg Supermicro report remains unverified and denied by the named parties, and it merged a hardware claim, an actor claim and a tasking claim into a single assertion, which is precisely the failure mode this database's per-variable confidence model exists to avoid. Firmware compromise and rogue device addition, by contrast, are routinely demonstrated.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Banks operate more security-critical hardware than almost any other commercial sector: HSMs, PIN pads, ATM dispensers and cash controllers, card personalisation equipment. Each has a supply chain, a repair loop and a decommissioning path, and each is handled by third parties. The realistic and demonstrated threats are firmware tampering during repair, terminal substitution in the field and rogue devices added inside offices. The exotic nation-state implant scenario absorbs disproportionate attention relative to its evidence base, and treating both at the same confidence level distorts spending.
ttps: Firmware modification during manufacture, repair or refurbishment
Interdiction and modification of equipment in shipping
Addition of rogue network devices by an insider or a visitor with premises access
Substitution of payment terminals and ATM components with modified units
Compromise of the vendor's own update and signing infrastructure
Exploitation of weak provenance controls in refurbished and grey-market hardware

existence.basis: Firmware tampering, rogue device addition and terminal substitution are well demonstrated; the server implant scenario is not.

attribution.basis: Very few incidents are attributed to a named actor; the most publicised claim remains unverified and denied.

financial_targeting.basis: ATM, HSM and payment terminal hardware is demonstrably targeted; general server implant targeting of finance is unevidenced.

state_tasking.basis: Asserted in reporting on the highest-profile case, never established.

watch_indicators: Firmware versions or hashes not matching the vendor's expected baseline
Serial numbers inconsistent with asset records after a repair cycle
Unexpected devices appearing on internal network segments
Equipment procured outside approved channels or from refurbishers
Tamper-evident seal discrepancies at installation or servicing

actors.name: Cable landing station and terrestrial fibre chokepoint exposure
actors.description: The shore end of the subsea cable system: landing stations, beach manholes, terrestrial backhaul and the small number of geographic chokepoints where many cables converge. More than 150 cable faults occur worldwide each year, with fishing and anchoring accounting for close to 70 percent, so deliberate sabotage is a small minority of a large number. That statistic cuts both ways. It means most outages are accidental, and it means a deliberate cut is easy to hide inside the noise. Landing stations are a far softer target than the cable itself: they are on land, few in number, and often lightly guarded.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Financial messaging, market data, inter-datacentre replication and cloud connectivity all depend on this infrastructure, and route diversity purchased from carriers frequently converges at the same landing station or the same duct without the buying institution knowing. That is the actual risk: not that a cable will be cut, but that an institution's documented diversity is fictional at the shore end. Repair timelines are governed by cable ship availability, which is a global constraint no customer can escalate.
ttps: Physical intrusion or damage at landing stations and beach manholes
Cutting of terrestrial backhaul in ducts and at aggregation points
Exploitation of chokepoints where many systems converge geographically
Concealment of deliberate damage within the high baseline of accidental faults
Targeting of repair and maintenance capacity, which is globally scarce

existence.basis: ICPC and carrier fault reporting; documented landing station security concerns in national reviews.

attribution.basis: Accidental and deliberate damage are difficult to distinguish; deliberate cases are rarely attributed.

financial_targeting.basis: Shared infrastructure with no finance-specific selection observed.

watch_indicators: Carrier fault notifications on routes carrying financial traffic
Discovery during diversity audit that nominally separate circuits share a landing station or duct
Repair vessel availability constraints published after a regional fault
Security incidents reported at landing stations serving the institution's routes
